extracted.intended_audience: Citizens of New York and the broader public deliberating the U.S. Constitution (readers considering ratification)
extracted.subtask_description: Federalist essays arguing for ratification of the proposed U.S. Constitution by showing how a stronger Union prevents interstate war, faction, commercial rivalry, standing armies, and foreign manipulation. Focused on the practical consequences of disunion and the protective benefits of a confederate republic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial disputes as a source of interstate hostility
rubrics_metrics.description: Territorial disputes have at all times been found one of the most fertile sources of hostility among nations; the United States has vast unsettled territory and discordant claims which disunion would revive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: conflicting claims to ungranted 'crown lands', Connecticut vs Pennsylvania (Wyoming), disputes over Western territory cessions. A federal umpire and cessions to the Union have so far helped appease controversies; dissolution of the Confederacy would reopen claims, provoke competing rules of apportionment, and create a theatre for hostile pretensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for a common umpire/judge to resolve interstate disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: In the wide field of Western territory there is ample theatre for hostile pretensions without any umpire or common judge to interpose between contending parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past recourse to federal courts (articles of confederation) produced decisions that required negotiation and equivalents to secure acquiescence; without an effective common authority, states may appeal to the sword.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitions of commerce breed contention
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate states pursuing different commercial policies will create distinctions, preferences, and exclusions that beget discontent; habits of equal privileges make perceived injuries sharper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific risk: a state (e.g., New York) imposing duties that effectively tax neighboring states' consumers, leading to resentment and potential reprisals. Infractions and efforts to prevent them lead to outrages and wars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial tributary relationships create resentment
rubrics_metrics.description: Opportunities for some states to render others tributary by commercial regulations will be impatiently submitted to by the tributary states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relative geographic/economic situations (example: NY vs CT and NJ) can cause sustained grievances over perceived exclusive benefits to one state's citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public debt apportionment will produce collision
rubrics_metrics.description: The apportionment and progressive extinguishment of a national public debt would be productive of ill-humor and animosity among separate states or confederacies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Difficulty agreeing on equitable rules of apportionment; differing views on national credit; creditors concentrated in some states will press for payment while others resist—delays, noncompliance, foreign pressure, and internal contention will follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws violating private contracts as cause of interstate retaliation
rubrics_metrics.description: State laws that impair private contracts of citizens of other states amount to aggressions that may provoke retaliation and hostility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical disposition to retaliation (example: Connecticut's reaction to 'enormities' by Rhode Island) shows that such legislative aggressions can lead to conflict unless constrained by federal checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incompatible foreign alliances magnify danger
rubrics_metrics.description: Different states or confederacies forming incompatible alliances with foreign nations would entangle America in European politics and make parts prey to foreign artifices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without a strong Union, 'divide et impera' becomes the motto of rival powers; a simple league would be too feeble to prevent dangerous entanglements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disunion produces standing armies and erosion of liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent war and constant apprehension in disunited states will produce standing armies and fortifications, which in turn strengthen executive power and tend toward monarchy and despotism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a country subject to internal invasions, armies must be numerous and continually maintained; this elevates military over civil power, weakens civil rights, and makes resistance to usurpation difficult. By contrast, a united, insulated situation reduces the need for large standing forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military establishments become engines of despotism
rubrics_metrics.description: Small or weaker states will adopt disciplined troops and fortifications to match more powerful neighbors; such expedients confer superiority and provoke others to follow, establishing the same engines of despotism found in Europe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standing armies increase the executive's importance at the expense of the legislature; history shows small vigorous governments with armies sometimes overcoming larger but less militarized states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlargement of the republic reduces faction and insurrection
rubrics_metrics.description: Extending the orbit of a popular government (by consolidating states into a larger confederate republic) is a means of repressing domestic faction and guarding internal tranquility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Montesquieu: a confederate republic preserves internal advantages of small republics while providing external force; a larger union allows reforming abuses in one part by the others, quelling insurrections, and preventing successful usurpation by a single member.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between confederacy and consolidation is largely practical
rubrics_metrics.description: A confederate republic is 'an assemblage of societies' whose federal authority's extent and objects are matters of discretion; preserving state organization for local purposes is compatible with strong national sovereignty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equal suffrage and restriction of national authority to collective objects are asserted by some opponents but are not absolute rules either by principle or precedent; the proposed Constitution preserves important portions of state sovereignty (e.g., Senate representation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Splitting larger states into smaller ones is a poor remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Dividing large states into many small jealous commonwealths would multiply petty offices, promote personal intrigue, and undermine greatness and happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The alternative of radical subdivision yields nursery republics of unceasing discord rather than a practical remedy for perceived problems of large states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security may justify temporary sacrifice of liberty in war
rubrics_metrics.description: The continual destruction and alarm of war will compel nations to resort for repose and security to institutions that have a tendency to destroy civil and political rights; thus safety can become the director of conduct at the expense of liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should weigh the trade-off: rejecting a Constitution on trivial objections risks long-term dangers that may force people to accept less freedom for security; therefore serious consideration of Union benefits is urged.
